paras: The Clinton wash-basin incident was a confrontation in late January 1903 at Clinton, Mississippi, in which Isham Peterson, a Black woodcutter, was driven from his white employer A. M. Gill's home after washing in Mrs. Gill's bowl. The local report said only that he was ordered off the premises, but a later Jackson dispatch claimed a hanging had narrowly been prevented. Both reports blamed President Roosevelt's racial policy.

According to a Clinton report dated January 27, Peterson was cutting wood for Gill, "one of our most respected citizens." When dinner time came, he went into Mrs. Gill's bedroom and washed his face and hands in her bowl. Questioned, he reportedly said that if Roosevelt ate with Booker T. Washington he saw no reason not to wash in her basin. Her husband then ordered him off the premises.

A Jackson dispatch credited to the Advocate told of an unnamed Clinton man hired to cut a cord of wood. In this version he washed in the family bowl at the dinner bell and "prepared to take dinner," and the ladies called for assistance. It said there "came near being a hanging," prevented "with the greatest difficulty," and that he could not say how he got out of the house.
No report of an arrest or charge appears in the coverage.

The Times-Promoter ran the Clinton report on January 30 under the headline "Fruits of Rooseveltism: Impudent Clinton Negro Attempts to Force Social Equality." On February 14 the New Iberia Enterprise in Louisiana reprinted the Jackson dispatch in an editorial, "Some More of the Fruits," pairing Clinton with a separate incident at Forest and blaming the "Roosevelt-Hays policy." It called the two men "candidates for 'glory' by the grape vine route" and tied the cases to the Indianola postoffice affair. No Black-press coverage of the incident was found.

The local report mentions only the husband's order to leave, while the second-hand dispatch describes a summoned group and a near-hanging. Only the Clinton report places him in the bedroom and quotes his remark about Roosevelt; only the dispatch says he prepared to take dinner.

bases: The local report has the man ordered off the premises without violence (A1), while a later dispatch says help was summoned and a hanging was narrowly prevented (A2); no injury or killing is reported in either.

Both reports agree that a Black woodcutter at Clinton washed in the household's bowl at dinner time and was driven out (A1, A2), but the local account describes only an order to leave (A1) while the later dispatch describes a near-hanging (A2).

accounts.label: Clinton correspondent (Jan. 27)
accounts.gist: Peterson washed in Mrs. Gill's bedroom bowl, answered her with a remark about Roosevelt dining with Booker T. Washington, and was immediately ordered off the premises by her husband.

accounts.label: Jackson press dispatch (credited to the Advocate)
accounts.gist: An unnamed Clinton woodcutter washed in the family bowl and prepared to take dinner; the ladies called for help, a hanging was prevented only with the greatest difficulty, and he got out of the house.

framing.detail: Headlined 'Fruits of Rooseveltism / Impudent Clinton Negro Attempts to Force Social Equality' and called the husband 'indignant' and 'one of our most respected citizens'.
Editorial 'Some More of the Fruits' called the two men 'candidates for "glory" by the grape vine route' and blamed the 'Roosevelt-Hays policy' and the Indianola postoffice incident.

versions.value: Ordered off the premises by the husband; no crowd or threat mentioned
Ladies called for help; a hanging came near and was prevented with the greatest difficulty; he got out of the house

conflicts.note: A1 is the local report, dated at Clinton three days earlier; A2 is a second-hand Jackson dispatch reprinted in a Louisiana editorial that pairs the case with another incident.

versions.value: Washed face and hands in Mrs. Gill's bowl in her bedroom
Walked into the house, washed hands in the family bowl and prepared to take dinner

conflicts.note: Only A2 says he prepared to take dinner; only A1 places him in the bedroom and reports his remark about Roosevelt.

record_check.dossier: On or shortly before 1903-01-27 (Clinton dateline Jan. 27); February is only the date of the Louisiana reprint.
No county is named in the papers; only Clinton, Miss.
No arms are mentioned; the local report has only an order to leave, the dispatch says help was summoned and a hanging nearly followed.
A. M. Gill ordered him off (A1); the dispatch names no one (A2).
Contested: the householder alone in the local report; unnamed people answering a call for help in the dispatch, with no number given.
Washing in Mrs. Gill's bowl, preparing to take dinner in the house, and a remark about Roosevelt dining with Booker T. Washington, framed as an attempt to 'force social equality'.

record_check.record: At Clinton, Mississippi, a Black man hired to cut wood ... a hanging was narrowly prevented, with the man escaping the house.
record_check.dossier: The near-hanging appears only in the second-hand dispatch; the earlier local report says he was ordered off the premises.

info: On or shortly before January 27, 1903 (Clinton dateline of Jan. 27); the later dispatch places it 'during the past week'.
The home of A. M. Gill at Clinton, Mississippi
Isham Peterson, a Black man hired to cut wood (named only in the local report; the dispatch leaves him unnamed)

Washing his face and hands in Mrs. Gill's bowl (A1) or the family bowl and preparing to take dinner in the house (A2); he is reported to have said that if Roosevelt ate with Booker T. Washington he saw no reason not to wash in her basin (A1).
A. M. Gill, who ordered him off the premises (A1); in the dispatch, unnamed people who answered the ladies' call for assistance (A2).
Peterson left the premises (A1); the dispatch says he got out of the house, he could not say exactly how (A2).

sources.note: Dated Clinton, Miss., Jan. 27: names Isham Peterson, cutting wood for A. M. Gill; washed in Mrs. Gill's bowl, cited Roosevelt and Booker T. Washington; ordered off the premises by the husband. No crowd or hanging mentioned.
quotes: he replied that if Mr. Roosevelt ate with Booker T. Washington he didn't see why he shouldn't wash in her basin.
The negro was immediately ordered off the premises by the indignant husband.
